To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the predictive ability of the CURB-65 and CRB-65 scores is limited in community-acquired pneumonia (CAP).
we developed and validated a model that predicts severe community-acquired pneumonia in adults.

1) community-acquired severity of pneumonia is not a binary variable; 2) community-acquired pneumonia is not a homogeneous entity; 3) community-acquired severe pneumonia can be predicted by clinical and radiographic features at presentation; and 4) the prediction of community-acquired severity is important for the selection of patients who should be treated with antibiotics that cover the causative pathogen.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of clinical and demographic factors that predict severity in children and adults with community-acquired pneumonia.
the development of a severity scoring system that will be useful for the prediction of community-acquired pneumonia (CAP).

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) severity prediction models are not ready to be used for clinical decision-making.
the current literature is not sufficient to allow for the development of a reliable and accurate severity prediction model in community-acquired pneumonia.
the current evidence does not allow to draw conclusions regarding the prognostic value of the severity scores for predicting outcome of patients with CAP.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown that the severity of illness in community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) can be predicted using a combination of easily obtained clinical variables and laboratory results.
we are predicting the risk of severe illness in community-acquired sepsis patients, not just the risk of mortality.
our study showed that community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) severity is a continuum and that the current severity stratification systems do not adequately reflect the true spectrum of disease severity.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the severity of community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) can be predicted by a simple score based on age and a few laboratory parameters.
the current definition of community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) is too broad and that the CAP severity prediction tools are not useful.
the use of the CURB-65 score in the emergency department (ED) to risk stratify patients with community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) is not supported by evidence.
